# Conclusion

Trust, in the setting this paper formalizes, is not a residual category
for whatever verification happens not to reach. Above a floor of two
physical residuals it factors into exactly three causes — determination,
certifiability, monotonicity — and the count is derived from what an
evidence scheme is rather than imposed on the cases. Each cause names an
anchor a verifier must rely on, and a repair priced in its own currency.
Two of the three axes live inside an algebra synthetic topology has
studied for four decades; the third was tested, and reported refuted, by
archival science's own empirical methods. No source this paper's sweep
reached composes them, or names their common complement as trust.

What is open is stated as open: the polynomial stratum, the
source-integrity instance's frontier tightness results, and the floor's
two residuals, which concern physical realization rather than the model
of @sec-model.

Two lines of work follow. The first is empirical: the full
source-integrity treatment — corroboration quorums, format and parse
gates, and the forced-generator tightness results the light instance of
@sec-instances omits by design — is conditional and prose-grade where
this paper is machine-checked, and belongs in its own venue.

The second is a diagnostic rather than a result, and is offered as such.
Machine-learned alignment resists verification on all three axes at
once: behavior on unseen inputs is not *determined* by any finite
training record; semantic behavioral properties are not *certifiable*,
by Rice–Shapiro; and an alignment claim over an open input space is
not *monotone*, since one adversarial input falsifies it after
arbitrarily much confirming evidence. Turning that into a theorem
requires pinning down what "aligned" means as a claim in this paper's
sense, which is not attempted here.
